author: Miles_Brundage
text: Probably the best version of the argument has to do with tradeoffs of time + attention + resourcing etc... but I just don't see that in practice. Like, my colleagues who worry more/less about different time horizons of risk want governments to do essentially *the same things.*

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
"They're just saying that their technology might kill everyone in order to fend off regulation" seems like a very implausible claim to me, and yet many believe it. 

What am I missing? Are there precedents for that tactic? How would regulating *less* help with the killing thing?

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
The cluster of issues around:

- Use of AI in influence operations + scams
- Watermarking/provenance for AI outputs
- Online proof of personhood

is definitely on the harder end of the spectrum as far as AI policy issues go.

Lots of collective action problems + tradeoffs.

author: Miles_Brundage
text:
Importantly, the idea of a "race to the bottom on safety" is a bit too abstract.

In the case of language models, safety should be broken down into at least few dimensions: 
- reliability
- steerability
- spontaneous bad stuff
- policies re: use cases
- general launch readiness
